questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: state what the photoelectric threshold implies about the delivery of light energy
questions.stem: Light of steadily rising frequency falls on a clean metal surface held in a vacuum, and the release of electrons is watched. What does the finding that emission begins only above one definite frequency establish about light?

options.text: Light hands over its energy in separate quanta, each of size set by the frequency

questions.explanation: The threshold is a sharp onset, not a gradual one, and a sharp onset is exactly what a packet picture predicts: an electron is handed one packet, and it escapes only if that single packet is worth at least the work function. A resonance or a waiting-time story would both predict a soft boundary, and a graded response is a property of the current, not of the threshold.

questions.topic: Nuclear radius trend across a table
questions.learningObjective: identify the scaling that connects nuclear radius to mass number
questions.stem: A table of measured nuclear radii runs 2.4 fm at mass number 8, 3.7 fm at 27, 4.8 fm at 64 and 6.0 fm at 125. Which single quantity accounts for the whole trend?

options.text: The cube root of the mass number, since added nucleons enlarge the volume not the radius
The mass number itself, since the radius should grow in direct proportion to it
options.misconception: expects a radius proportional to the nucleon count, which would be far too large

options.text: The square root of the mass number, taken from a surface to volume argument
options.misconception: uses the wrong power of the mass number, so no single constant survives

options.text: The atomic number, since it is the added charge that pushes the surface out
options.misconception: attributes the radius trend to charge rather than to the nucleon count

questions.explanation: Dividing each radius by the cube root of its mass number gives about 1.2 fm every time, and that single constant is the whole explanation: nucleons crowd into a nearly fixed volume per nucleon, so extra nucleons grow the volume and the radius follows its cube root. Direct proportion would predict a radius of 30 fm at mass number 125 rather than 6.0 fm, and a square root would fit none of the rows exactly. The charge count plays no part in the size, which is why light and heavy nuclei of the same mass number are the same size.
questions.hint: Divide each radius by a candidate power of the mass number and see which stays constant.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: judge what a measured pair of spreads does and does not establish
questions.stem: Repeated trials on one prepared electron give a position spread of 1.0e-10 m and a momentum spread of 5.3e-25 kg m per second. Using a Planck constant of 6.626e-34 J s, what does the product of the two spreads establish?

options.text: It sits just above the floor, so the state is allowed and near the minimum but not required to be
It lies below the floor, so the two measurements cannot both be correct
options.misconception: treats a floor as an exact equality that every measured pair must match

options.text: It lies far above the floor, so extra classical noise must have been added
options.misconception: assumes any excess over the floor is instrumental rather than physical

options.text: It fixes the electron mass, since the constant in the bound contains that mass
options.misconception: believes the constant in the bound carries the particle mass in it

questions.explanation: The floor is the Planck constant over four pi, which is 5.27e-35 in these units, and the measured product of 5.3e-35 is just above it, so the state is allowed and happens to be close to the minimum case without any obligation to be there. A measured product below the floor would be a real crisis, since it would mean the relation does not hold, but a product a little above it is the most ordinary outcome in physics. A product far above the floor would say the state is a mixture of momenta, not that an instrument was faulty, and the constant in the bound is the Planck constant alone.
questions.hint: Compare the product with the Planck constant over four pi before drawing a conclusion.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the stopping potential is a maximum
questions.learningObjective: explain why the stopping potential measures a maximum kinetic energy
questions.stem: A metal emits electrons under light, and a retarding potential is raised until the current stops. Explain in your own words why the potential that finally stops the current corresponds to the largest kinetic energy rather than to a typical one.

answer.exemplar: The electrons leaving the surface do not all come away with the same energy, because the ones nearer the surface lose less on the way out than the ones that have to travel further through the material, and because the surface itself is not perfectly flat. The retarding field does not act on them all equally: it turns back the fastest ones first, so the current falls gradually as the potential is raised and the faster groups are removed one at a time. The current only reaches zero when the field is strong enough to turn back the very fastest electron that ever left, so the potential at that point equals that electron's kinetic energy. That is why it is called a stopping potential: it is the threshold of the sweep, which is exactly why a statement about the average energy of the emitted electrons cannot be read off from it, and why the fall of current with voltage is a curve rather than a single sudden drop.

questions.explanation: The retarding field sorts electrons by speed, so the potential at which the current vanishes is set by the extreme of the distribution rather than by its middle. The fall of current is gradual for the same reason, and that curve is the measurement of the distribution itself.
questions.hint: Ask which electrons the field removes first as the potential is raised.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the duality statement concerns description rather than the particle
questions.stem: Textbooks say an electron is both a wave and a particle. Explain why that wording is a statement about how the electron is described and predicted, and not a claim that the electron itself is two things at once.

answer.exemplar: The two descriptions are two pieces of mathematics that answer two different questions, and the theory is not asking which one is the real electron. A prediction of where the next electron will land on a screen is built from amplitudes that interfere, so the wave side is what makes a fringe pattern predictable, and there is no way to get those probabilities out of a rule that says each electron simply follows a line. Once the electron is registered, though, the arrival is a single localised event, and a rule that smeared it over the whole screen would be wrong about that. Neither description is a picture of a small object, and the electron is not a wave that turns into a particle at the moment of detection: the switch is in which question is being asked, and the same single state predicts both results without any change to the electron in between.

questions.explanation: A state that predicts interference and then a single localised arrival is one state, not a particle that mutates. The choice of description follows the question being asked, and the physics does not depend on which is chosen.
questions.hint: Ask whether the choice of description is made by the question or by the particle.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which which-path information destroys an interference pattern
questions.stem: A marker beside a double slit can record which opening a particle used, and adding it makes the interference fringes disappear. Explain what has changed about the two paths, and why the effect does not require the marker to push the particle about.

answer.exemplar: Interference comes from adding the two route amplitudes before anything is recorded, and fringes exist only while the two routes cannot be told apart. The marker is a place where the route is remembered: it is a physical record of which opening was used, and once that record exists the two route amplitudes can no longer be added as alternatives, because the alternatives have become distinguishable facts about the world. The probabilities then add instead of the amplitudes, and the sum of two nonnegative quantities has no cancellation in it, so the minima fill in and only a plain mixture of two single-slit patterns is left. Nothing need touch the particle for this to happen, which is why a marker far too weak to deflect it still works, and why the pattern returns unchanged if the record is erased before the arrival is registered.

questions.explanation: Distinguishable routes give probabilities that add; indistinguishable routes give amplitudes that interfere. The availability of the record, not any mechanical disturbance, is what removes the cancellation.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the amplitudes once the route is stored somewhere.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the ground state is the lowest energy
questions.learningObjective: explain why the ground state of hydrogen is the lowest energy available to the electron
questions.stem: Hydrogen has a lowest allowed energy, and a photon below about 13.6 eV cannot remove the electron no matter how many are absorbed. Explain where that floor comes from, and what the electron would have to do to get past it.

answer.exemplar: The levels are fixed by the balance between the attraction of the electron to the proton and the kinetic energy the electron carries as it moves. As the orbit is made smaller the attraction rises steeply, but the kinetic energy rises faster, because a confined particle of shorter wavelength is a faster one, and the sum of the two has a minimum rather than decreasing without limit. That minimum is the ground state, the value of 13.6 eV below an electron at rest outside the atom. Getting past the floor therefore cannot be done by shrinking the orbit, since that costs energy rather than saving it, and it cannot be done by adding energy in pieces either, because nothing between the ground state and the continuum exists. The energy has to arrive in one quantum carrying at least 13.6 eV, which is why a stream of soft photons adds nothing at all.

questions.explanation: The floor is a minimum of the total energy, not a barrier that shrinking the orbit lowers. One photon must carry the whole binding energy, which is why soft light of any total energy fails.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the kinetic energy as the orbit is made smaller.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain the meaning of a half-life as a per-nucleus probability
questions.stem: A sample is described as having a half-life of a few days, yet the nuclei in it do not decay on a schedule or share a signal. Explain what the half-life actually states, and what it does not state about any individual nucleus.

answer.exemplar: The half-life is a statement about a rate, and rates are properties of populations rather than of individuals. It says that for any large number of identical nuclei, the expected number left undecayed falls to half after that interval, which remains true whether the sample holds a billion nuclei or a million, and it says nothing about when any one of them will go. An individual nucleus either decays or it does not, with a fixed chance per unit time, and the waiting time is spread out over the whole life of the sample rather than being booked in advance. That is why a small sample gives a much more ragged history than the quoted number, and why a larger sample follows the half-life closely while a smaller one appears to have none. The half-life is also fixed by the nucleus alone, so it is unaffected by pressure, temperature or chemical form, all of which change the surroundings but not the nucleus.

questions.explanation: The quantity is statistical, so it constrains large populations and leaves individual events unpredictable. Only the rate is shared, never the schedule.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement can be made about one nucleus or only about many.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The uncertainty relation is not an instrument defect
questions.learningObjective: explain why the uncertainty relation is a property of states rather than of apparatus
questions.stem: The uncertainty relation is often described as saying that measurement disturbs the system. Explain why that description mislocates the limit, and why the limit cannot be pushed away by building a better instrument.

answer.exemplar: The limit is a statement about which states can be prepared, and it can be run entirely as an argument about wave patterns with no apparatus in the room at all. A state with a well-defined position is a wave with a short wavelength spread, and a short wavelength spread is a wide spread of momenta, because momentum is proportional to the reciprocal of the wavelength. Sharpening the position therefore forces a wider momentum spread inside the state itself, before anything is measured, and the constant in the bound is just what fixes how sharp the trade can be. This is why a state prepared with a very small momentum spread has a large position spread whether or not anybody looks at it, and why the same pair of numbers comes out of repeated trials on an untouched state. A better instrument measures the two spreads more accurately, and can even pin the position of a given particle to a fine grid, but it cannot turn a state with a wide momentum spread into one with a narrow spread, because that state was never prepared.

questions.explanation: The trade-off lives in the state and is fixed by the wave character of the preparation, so improving the measurement changes the accuracy and not the physics.
questions.hint: Argue the bound from a wave with a narrow wavelength spread, with no apparatus involved.

questions.learningObjective: order the steps that produce a measured stopping potential
questions.stem: Four statements describe how a laboratory measures the stopping potential for a metal. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The retarding potential is raised in steps and the current is recorded at each step
The current is plotted against the retarding potential and the zero crossing is located
Light of a known frequency falls on the cleaned surface inside the evacuated tube
The largest kinetic energy is read off that graph and compared with the photon energy

questions.explanation: Nothing can be recorded until electrons exist, so the light goes on first, and the frequency has to be known before the comparison at the end means anything. The sweep of the retarding potential then generates the data, and the graph of current against potential is what locates the voltage at which the last electron is turned back. Reading the largest energy off that graph and comparing it with the photon energy is the analysis that follows the measurement, so the order runs from the source, to the sweep, to the graph, to the comparison. Reversing the first two steps is impossible because there is no current to sweep before the light is on.
questions.hint: A current has to exist before it can be swept, and the comparison comes last.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: From a diffraction pattern to a wavelength
questions.learningObjective: order the reasoning that extracts a matter wavelength from a diffraction pattern
questions.stem: Four statements describe how an electron diffraction pattern is turned into a number for the matter wavelength. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: The ring radius is measured and the angle to the direct beam is calculated
The momentum follows from the accelerating voltage and the de Broglie relation
An electron beam of known accelerating voltage is scattered by the crystal film
The spacing of the crystal planes and that angle give the wavelength

questions.explanation: The beam has to exist and interact with the lattice before there is any pattern at all, so the scattering comes first, and the known accelerating voltage is what will later tie the wavelength to a momentum. The geometry of the pattern is then measured, since the ring radius sets the angle between the direct beam and the scattered one. The diffraction condition relates that angle to the wavelength in terms of the plane spacing, and only after the wavelength is in hand does the de Broglie relation convert it into a momentum for comparison with the accelerating voltage. The reverse order is impossible because the pattern carries no information about the lattice until the interaction that uses the lattice has happened.
questions.hint: The measurement gives geometry, the geometry gives a wavelength, and only then a momentum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: order the steps in computing a Compton wavelength shift
questions.stem: Four statements describe how the wavelength of a photon after a Compton scattering event is calculated. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: The product of the Planck constant and the electron mass over mass times speed is evaluated
The scattered wavelength is the incident wavelength plus that constant times one minus cosine
The incident wavelength and the scattering angle are read from the problem
The energy given to the recoil electron is the difference between the two photon energies

questions.explanation: The two pieces of information the calculation needs, the incident wavelength and the angle, come from the statement of the problem, and until both are known there is nothing to evaluate. The natural constant that sets the size of the effect is then computed, and that constant times one minus the cosine of the angle gives the shift, which is added to the incident wavelength to reach the scattered one. Only when both photon energies exist can the energy handed to the recoil electron be taken as the difference between them, and putting that step earlier would require a scattered energy that has not been found. The constant is a property of the electron, not of the photon, which is why it is evaluated before the photon is tracked.
questions.hint: Inputs first, then the constant, then the shift, then the energy difference.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: From a count rate to a decay constant
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that turn two count rates into a decay constant
questions.stem: Four statements describe how a decay constant is extracted from two count rates taken at different times. Put them in the order in which they occur, earliest first.

options.text: That half-life is the elapsed time divided by the number of halvings, which is here 3.0 hours
The ratio of the two count rates is examined to find how many halvings have passed
The decay constant is the natural logarithm of 2 divided by that half-life, giving 0.231 per hour
The earlier and later count rates are read from the log, 8000 and 500 per second

questions.explanation: The two readings are the raw material, so they come off the log first, and their ratio of sixteen is then examined to see that it represents four halvings rather than sixteen of them or one. That count of halvings converts an elapsed time into a half-life, which is 12.0 hours over four, and the decay constant is the logarithm of 2 divided by that half-life, 0.231 per hour. The inversion trap sits in the last step: the half-life is a time and the constant is a rate, so dividing the logarithm of 2 by the half-life is the only one of the two orderings that carries units of reciprocal time.
questions.hint: Readings, then the number of halvings, then the half-life, then the rate.
